```{r}
#| include: false
require(mosaic)
require(gridExtra)
require(abd)
require(Lock5withR)
myxs = rexp(20, 0.2)
```

# Some quantitative data from an unknown source

```{r}
myxs
```

I wish to make inferences about $\mu$, the
mean of the population from which this sample
was drawn, using these values.  The size of
the sample:

```{r}
length(myxs)
```

The sample size is smaller than 30, and a
normal quantile plot does not reassure us that
the population is normal
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 2.5
gf_qq(~myxs)
```

A histogram of the data values shows a distinct
right-skew.
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 2.5
gf_histogram(~myxs, bins=10)
```

# Transforming data

Data that is right skewed and positive-valued
might be "compacted", becoming more symmetric,
using transformations such as

$$ y = x^r, \qquad\mbox{where}\qquad 0 < r < 1, $$
or by
$$ y = \log(x). $$
Using log(), our data looks reasonably normal
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 2.5
gf_histogram(~log(myxs), bins=10)
```

How to use to estimate $\mu$?
```{r}
sampleLogMean = mean(~log(myxs))
s = sd(~log(myxs))
tstar = qt(.975, df=19)     # for 95% confidence
marginOfError = tstar*s/sqrt(20)
sampleLogMean + c(-1,1)*marginOfError
```

This is a 95% confidence interval for $\log(\mu)$,
not for $\mu$ itself.  We use these bounds, but
reverse the log transformation to obtain bounds
for $\mu$:
```{r}
exp(c(1.125, 1.971))
```

# Matched-pairs data

In the Lock5withR package there is a data set
called `Wetsuits`.  Each swimmer is a case
providing matched pairs data, a maximum velocity
swimming 1500 m in a Wetsuit, and a maximum
velocity swimming the event in on non wetsuit.
We build a 1-sample $t$ CI on the differences
$$ \mbox{Wetsuit} - \mbox{NoWetsuit}, $$
```{r}
xbar = mean(~(Wetsuit - NoWetsuit), data=Wetsuits)
sampleSD = sd(~(Wetsuit - NoWetsuit), data=Wetsuits)
tstar = qt(0.975, df = length(Wetsuits) - 1)
xbar + c(-1,1)*tstar*sampleSD
```

I have neglected verifying that the sampling
distribution of $\bar X$ is plausibly normal.
There is inadequate sample size to rubber-stamp
this.  And a normal quantile plot falls quite
short of convincing us that the population is
normal:
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 2.5
gf_qq(~(Wetsuit - NoWetsuit), data=Wetsuits)
```

# Sign Test

We might change our goal, giving up on estimating
the mean difference.  Instead, we might simply
look at each instance where the difference is
positive as a "success", and each instance where
the difference is negative as a "failure".
We use the `sign()` function to determine how
many successes/failures there are.
```{r}
sign(Wetsuits$Wetsuit - Wetsuits$NoWetsuit)
```
These can be viewed as binomial counts.  We test
how likely it is to see 12 successes out of 12
in a world where this difference has equal chance
of being positive or negative:
```{r}
binom.test(12, 12)
```

This "sign test" is an hypothesis test.  The
$p$-value of $0.00048$ leads to our rejecting
that the chance of swimming faster in a wetsuit
is merely 50%.
